title: April Dunford, An Introduction to Positioning
text:
## What positioning is

April Dunford defines positioning as: "Positioning defines how your product is a leader at delivering something that a well-defined set of customers cares a lot about." Positioning is not a tagline, a slogan, or a brand color palette. It is the deliberate act of choosing the context in which a product is understood, so that its value becomes obvious to the right buyers.

## Positioning is context-setting

Dunford compares positioning to the opening scene of a movie. The opening establishes where and when the story takes place and what is happening, so the audience knows how to interpret everything that follows. Positioning does the same job for a product: it orients customers by answering fundamental questions about what the product is and who it is for, before they evaluate any specific feature. Without that context, a strong product can look confusing, boring, or irrelevant. With the right context, the same product looks obviously awesome.

## The five components of positioning

Dunford identifies five essential building blocks that together form a product's positioning:

1. Competitive Alternatives: what customers would use or do if your product did not exist. This is the reference point that makes everything else meaningful.
2. Differentiated Features or Capabilities: the unique attributes you have that the alternatives do not.
3. Value for Customers: the benefit that the differentiated capabilities enable, expressed as something customers actually care about.
4. Target Customer Segmentation: the specific customers who care a lot about that value, described by characteristics that make them a best fit.
5. Market Category: the market context you place the product in so the value is obvious to the target customer, and which frames customer expectations.

## Why the order and relationships matter

Dunford stresses that great positioning is achieved when all five components are defined in the best possible way for the offering, and that each component depends on the others. Your unique value is only meaningful relative to differentiated features, which are only differentiated relative to the competitive alternatives, and your best-fit customers are the ones who care most about that unique value. Positioning is the foundation beneath storytelling, messaging, taglines, vision, and branding: it determines which market you choose to compete in and why you deserve to win it. Get positioning wrong and every downstream marketing artifact inherits the mistake.

title: April Dunford, A Quickstart Guide to Positioning (the process)
text:
## The positioning process, in order

April Dunford's method works the five components in a deliberate sequence, because each one builds on the last.

### Step 1: Competitive Alternatives
Start here. Ask what customers would do or use if your solution did not exist. The honest answer is often a spreadsheet, a manual process, hiring an intern, or simply doing nothing and living with the problem. Dunford warns against "phantom competitors": theoretical rivals you never actually see or lose to in real deals. Only include alternatives customers genuinely evaluate, because these alternatives are the baseline against which your differentiation is judged.

### Step 2: Key Unique Attributes
Ask "What do we have that the alternatives do not?" List the differentiated capabilities or features that your product has and the competitive alternatives lack. Differentiation only exists relative to the alternatives named in step 1.

### Step 3: Value Themes
Ask "So what for customers?" Translate each unique capability into the concrete value it delivers. In Dunford's Janna Systems example, the capability to model relationships in a different way translated into letting companies get insight into interpersonal relationships for a sales advantage.

### Step 4: Target Market Characteristics
Identify the customers who care most intensely about your differentiated value, because certain customers care a lot more than others. Describe the characteristics that signal a strong fit. For Janna, investment banking and private client services were ideal because they relied heavily on personal relationships.

### Step 5: Market Category
Choose the context you position the product in so your value is obvious to the target customer. Dunford calls the market category the definition of the market you intend to win. You can compete in an existing category or create a new one.

## The Janna Systems example

Janna was generically positioned as "Enterprise CRM" and competing head to head against Siebel Systems. Working the process surfaced a unique attribute (modeling relationships differently), a value (sales insight into interpersonal dynamics and deal influence), and a best-fit segment (investment banks and private client firms). Repositioned as "CRM for Investment Banks," revenue grew from under 2 million dollars to close to 80 million dollars in 18 months.

## Anti-pattern: the category-creation myth

Creating a brand new market category looks glamorous but usually underperforms. Dunford notes that about 90 percent of tech companies that went public over the past five years were positioned in existing markets, not new categories. Successful companies typically start by positioning in an existing category until they have the money and momentum to try to shift or expand category boundaries later. Do not reach for category creation as a default; earn the right to it.

title: Avinash Kaushik, See-Think-Do-Care: A Business Framework for Marketing and Measurement
text:
## See-Think-Do-Care: intent clusters, not a funnel

Avinash Kaushik's See-Think-Do-Care framework organizes marketing around audience intent clusters rather than a traditional Awareness to Purchase funnel. The core unit is the Largest Addressable Qualified Audience (LAQA): people whose behavior demonstrates relevant intent, where the critical letter is Q for qualified, because qualification comes primarily from behavior, not demographics.

## The four intent clusters

See: the largest qualified audience, with no commercial intent. These are people engaged with topics aligned to your business but not in a buying mindset. Example given: health conscious people who want to improve their lifestyle.

Think: a smaller audience showing weak commercial intent. They are comparing options, researching alternatives, and evaluating solutions.

Do: the smallest audience with strong commercial intent, close to making a purchase. Signals include shopping cart activity, checkout, and purchase-ready keywords.

Care: existing customers who are extra loyal, with two or more purchases or long-term revenue relationships. Care is about deepening the relationship with utility and value, not just reselling.

## Content, then marketing, then measurement

Kaushik insists the framework forces evaluation of the complete business strategy: you need content, marketing, and measurement working together for each cluster. See content informs, entertains, or provides utility with no sales pressure. Think content educates about solutions and positions your unique value. Do content is optimized for the purchase decision and addresses final objections. Care content provides ongoing value to loyal customers and is rarely implemented well.

## Channels differ by intent

Different platforms attract different clusters. See intent lives in YouTube, organic and paid brand building on social, and blog consumption. Think intent responds to display, retargeting, comparison content, and email nurturing. Do intent is captured by search ads on purchase keywords, product pages, and checkout optimization. Care intent is served by segmented email programs, exclusive content, and customer communities.

## Metrics mapped to each cluster

See metrics: interaction rate, amplification, and community growth. Think metrics: assisted conversions, engagement depth, and consideration lift. Do metrics: conversion rate, cost per acquisition, and transaction value. Care metrics: lifetime value, repeat purchase rate, advocacy or Net Promoter signals, and churn reduction.

## Why traditional funnels fail

The framework rejects the linear Awareness, Consideration, Purchase, Loyalty model because it ignores the See stage entirely, narrows Care to repeat sales rather than relationship building, and wrongly assumes customers move in a tidy line. Common failure modes: running ads without content is "ads writing cheques your website can't cash"; content without paid amplification lacks scale; and measurement without strategy is useless.

title: Strategyzer (Alexander Osterwalder), The Value Proposition Canvas
text:
## The Value Proposition Canvas

Strategyzer's Value Proposition Canvas, created by Alexander Osterwalder and colleagues, is a tool for designing products and services customers actually want. It has two interconnected sides that you work to bring into alignment.

## The Customer Profile

The Customer Profile describes a specific customer segment in detail through three elements:

Customer Jobs (Jobs-to-be-Done): the tasks customers are trying to get done, the problems they are trying to solve, or the needs they are trying to satisfy. Jobs can be functional, social, or emotional.

Pains: the bad outcomes, risks, and obstacles customers face when trying to accomplish their jobs. These are the frustrations, undesired costs and situations, and risks that could go wrong.

Gains: the outcomes and benefits customers want, including required, expected, desired, and unexpected gains. These are the results and benefits customers perceive from getting their jobs done.

## The Value Map

The Value Map describes how your offering creates value for that segment, also through three elements:

Products and Services: the list of what you offer that helps the customer get a job done.

Pain Relievers: how your products and services relieve specific customer pains, removing or reducing the bad outcomes and obstacles.

Gain Creators: how your products and services create the specific gains the customer wants.

## Fit

Fit is achieved when the Value Map addresses the most important jobs, the most extreme pains, and the most relevant gains in the Customer Profile. You reach problem-solution fit when you have evidence that customers care about the jobs, pains, and gains you address, and product-market fit when the market responds to your value proposition. The canvas is designed to be tested and adjusted based on customer evidence, not assumptions.

title: Philip Kotler (American Marketing Association), A Lifetime in Marketing: STP and the Marketing Mix
text:
## Marketing is about creating value

Philip Kotler, the author of Marketing Management and the person who systematized modern marketing, centers his philosophy on creating and delivering customer value, not merely selling products. The company aims to satisfy or delight its target customers, a customer-centric orientation that replaced the older product-centric and selling-centric views.

## STP is the essence of strategic marketing

Kotler frames Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning (STP) as the strategic heart of marketing. The company uses STP to choose its target customers: segmentation partitions the market by criteria such as demographics, geography, psychographics, and behavior; targeting selects which segments to serve; positioning defines how the offering should be perceived in the minds of those target customers relative to competitors. Kotler advises selecting markets where the company can be strong on the 4As: Awareness, Acceptability, Affordability, and Accessibility.

## The marketing planning sequence

Kotler lays out the planning flow as Marketing Research, then Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning, then defining the Target Market and the Value Proposition, then the Marketing Plan, then Implementation and Control. STP comes first and sets up everything downstream.

## The 4Ps and their evolution

Kotler popularized the 4Ps marketing mix: Product, Price, Place, and Promotion. STP provides the who and the why (strategic), while the 4Ps provide the what, how much, where, and how you communicate (tactical). STP is done first and the 4Ps implement it. Kotler has since argued for expanding the mix, adding components such as Service, Brand, and Incentives to better reflect how companies create value. He also describes Marketing 3.0, a values-driven marketing that is purpose-led, respectful of the environment, and aimed at human happiness.

title: IPA, The Key Works of Les Binet and Peter Field (The Long and the Short of It)
text:
## The evidence base

Les Binet and Peter Field analyzed the IPA Databank, roughly 996 campaigns entered into the IPA Effectiveness Awards between 1980 and 2010, to find what actually drives sustained business results. Their landmark 2013 report, The Long and the Short of It, is the origin of the modern brand-building versus sales-activation distinction.

## Two jobs: brand building and sales activation

Brand building is broad-reach, emotionally resonant, long-term work that creates and refreshes memory structures, builds mental availability, and grows the base of future demand. Its effects are slow to build but compound and are durable. Sales activation is targeted, usually rational or promotional, short-term work that converts existing demand into sales now. Its effects are sharp but decay quickly. The two work on different time horizons and must both be funded.

## The 60/40 rule

The IPA data indicates the optimum long-run balance is around 60 percent of budget on brand building and 40 percent on sales activation. Campaigns near this split outperformed those skewed heavily to either end, and the advantage showed up not only in short-term sales but in sustained market share, profit margins, and pricing power. Subsequent research (Effectiveness in Context) refined the optimum to about 62/38, and the ratio varies by category and channel.

## Excess Share of Voice (ESOV)

A central mechanism is Share of Voice versus Share of Market. When a brand's Share of Voice (its share of category advertising) exceeds its Share of Market, that Excess Share of Voice (ESOV) tends to drive market share growth over time; when SOV is below SOM, the brand tends to shrink. ESOV links advertising investment to growth in a measurable way.

## Anti-pattern: short-termism

Binet and Field's central warning is against short-termism: an over-focus on efficiency, tight targeting, and short-term metrics (like immediate ROI and last-click conversions) at the expense of scale, reach, and long-term brand building. Chasing only the measurable, immediate response starves the brand-building that produces the largest and most durable profits, and erodes pricing power. Effectiveness requires balancing the long and the short, not choosing one.

title: Al Ries and Jack Trout, Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind (summary of the seminal work)
text:
## Positioning is done to the mind, not the product

Al Ries and Jack Trout's central idea is that positioning is what you do to the mind of the prospect, not what you do to the product. A company creates a position in the prospect's mind that reflects its own strengths and weaknesses and those of its competitors. You do not change the product; you change perception.

## The overcommunicated society

We live in an overcommunicated society where very little communication actually gets through. The volume of messages has exploded, so the mind screens and rejects most of what it is offered. The winning response is the oversimplified message: in communication, as in architecture, less is more. You must sharpen your message to cut into the mind, eliminate ambiguities, and repeat a simple concept.

## The Law of Leadership: be first in the mind

Being first in the prospect's mind is the single most powerful position. It is better to be first than it is to be better. The leader should reinforce its original concept rather than merely attack competitors. Leaders own a word or position, like the number-one brand people recall in a category.

## If you cannot be first, create a category you can be first in

When you cannot dominate an existing category, find a hole and establish a new category where you can be first. Look for gaps in the marketplace and in the prospect's mind rather than fighting a superior incumbent head on.

## The ladder in the mind

Consumers arrange brands on a mental ladder within each category, with the leader on the top rung. Your positioning strategy depends on which rung you occupy. A challenger should relate itself to the leader rather than ignore it (the against-position, as in Avis "We're number two, we try harder").

## Repositioning the competition

To move into an occupied mind, you often must reposition the competitor: change what people believe about the incumbent so a space opens for you. This is done by shifting perception, not by claiming you are simply better.

## Anti-pattern: the line-extension trap

Ries and Trout warn against line extension, stretching a strong brand name across many products. It usually weakens the position because a name that stands for everything stands for nothing in the mind. They favor using distinct brand names for distinct positions.

title: Ehrenberg-Bass Institute (John Dawes), Advertising Effectiveness and the 95-5 Rule
text:
## The 95-5 rule

Professor John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute established the 95-5 rule: at any given time, approximately 95 percent of business buyers are not actively purchasing in a category, and only about 5 percent are in-market. As Dawes puts it, up to 95 percent of business clients are not in the market for many goods and services at any one time.

## Why the numbers look this way

Inter-purchase cycles in B2B are long. Corporations typically change major service providers, like their principal bank or law firm, roughly every five years. That implies only about 20 percent of buyers purchase in a given year, and about 5 percent in a given quarter for a 90-day sales cycle.

## What advertising actually does

Because most ad exposure reaches people who are not buying right now, advertising cannot primarily drive immediate sales. Dawes argues that advertising mostly works by building and refreshing memory links to the brand, and these memory links activate later when buyers do come into the market. The job is to be remembered at the future moment of need.

## Mental availability and Category Entry Points

The strategic goal is mental availability: the degree to which potential buyers associate a brand with the relevant buying situations, called Category Entry Points (CEPs). Building strong mental availability requires multi-year, broad-reach effort. Even market leaders typically achieve only around 50 percent mental availability among their target audience, so there is almost always room to grow by linking the brand to more CEPs.

## Anti-pattern: only chasing the in-market 5 percent

Focusing exclusively on the ready-to-buy 5 percent (pure lead-gen and bottom-funnel targeting) limits long-term growth. Successful brands advertise continuously to out-of-market audiences to build familiarity and memory structures before the purchase occasion arises, so they are already known and considered when the buyer finally enters the market.

title: Theodore Levitt, Marketing Myopia (encyclopedic summary of the 1960 HBR classic)
text:
## The core thesis

Marketing Myopia, Theodore Levitt's 1960 Harvard Business Review article, argues that businesses fail when they define their market too narrowly, focusing on their product rather than the underlying customer need. This short-sightedness causes them to miss growth and eventually decline. Levitt's most quoted claim: there is no such thing as a growth industry, there are only companies organized and operated to create and capitalize on growth opportunities.

## The railroad example

The railroads did not stop growing because the need for passenger and freight transportation declined; that need grew. They faltered because they thought they were in the railroad business rather than the transportation business. They were railroad-oriented instead of transportation-oriented, and product-oriented instead of customer-oriented. So they let others (cars, trucks, airplanes) take their customers.

## The buggy-whip and Hollywood examples

Levitt uses the buggy-whip maker: had it defined itself as in the transportation business (or the vehicle-starter business) rather than the buggy-whip business, it might have survived the arrival of the automobile. Hollywood nearly destroyed itself by defining its business as movies rather than entertainment; television should have been an opportunity, not a threat, had studios seen themselves in the entertainment business.

## Product orientation versus customer orientation, and selling versus marketing

The cure is to shift from a product orientation to a customer orientation: start from the customer's needs and work backward, rather than starting from the product and pushing it. Levitt draws the line between selling and marketing: selling focuses on the needs of the seller (converting product into cash), marketing on the needs of the buyer (satisfying the customer through the whole cluster of things associated with creating, delivering, and consuming the product).

## Root causes of myopia

Levitt names conditions that breed complacency: the belief that growth is assured by an expanding population, the belief that there is no competitive substitute for the industry's main product, over-faith in mass production and falling unit costs, and a preoccupation with a product that lends itself to scientific experimentation and improvement rather than to serving the customer. Some oil companies partially corrected by redefining themselves as being in the energy business rather than only petroleum.

title: Byron Sharp, How Brands Grow: the empirical laws (faithful summary)
text:
## Growth comes from penetration, not loyalty

Byron Sharp and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute show, from repeated empirical data, that brands grow primarily by increasing penetration, the number of people who buy the brand, rather than by increasing loyalty among existing buyers. Market share is driven far more by how many buyers you have than by how often each buyer buys.

## The Double Jeopardy Law

Smaller brands get hit twice: they have fewer buyers, and those buyers are slightly less loyal (buy the brand a little less often). Larger brands have more buyers who are slightly more loyal. Loyalty differences between brands are small and follow from market share, so you cannot build a big brand by chasing loyalty alone; you must acquire more buyers.

## Pareto and light buyers

Sharp refines the Pareto principle: roughly the top 20 percent of a brand's buyers account for about 50 percent of sales, and the lightest 50 percent of buyers account for around 20 percent. Crucially, light and non-buyers are the largest growth opportunity, so marketing must reach all category buyers, not just heavy loyalists.

## Mental and physical availability

Brands grow by building mental availability (being easy to bring to mind in buying situations, via memory structures linked to Category Entry Points) and physical availability (being easy to find and buy, via broad distribution and presence). Sharp notes that around 80 percent or more distribution is necessary, though not sufficient, for high market share.

## Distinctive brand assets and reach

Brands should be distinctive rather than differentiated: build and consistently use distinctive brand assets (colors, logos, characters, sounds) that trigger the brand from memory. The Duplication of Purchase Law shows brands share customers in line with market share, so all brands in a category compete with each other regardless of positioning. The practical prescriptions are continuous broad-reach advertising, sophisticated mass marketing, and reaching the whole category rather than narrow niches.

## Anti-pattern: over-investing in loyalty and heavy buyers

Sharp's evidence contradicts the common belief that retention and loyalty programs are the cheapest path to growth. Because customer bases seldom vary (your customers look like your competitors' customers) and defection is roughly a function of size, growth requires continuous acquisition and reach, not loyalty schemes aimed at existing heavy buyers.

title: Kevin Lane Keller, Customer-Based Brand Equity (CBBE) Pyramid
text:
## The CBBE pyramid

Kevin Lane Keller's Customer-Based Brand Equity model, from his 1993 Journal of Marketing work, holds that brand equity exists in how customers think, feel, and act toward a brand. It is a four-level pyramid, and each level answers a question the customer implicitly asks. You must secure each level before the next.

## Level 1: Brand Salience (identity), Who are you?

The foundation is brand awareness, its depth and breadth: how easily and in what situations customers recall or recognize the brand. This is about achieving mental availability at moments of need and the right breadth of category entry points.

## Level 2: Brand Meaning (performance and imagery), What are you?

Meaning is built from two parallel blocks. Brand Performance is how well the product meets functional needs: quality, reliability, features, service effectiveness, and value. Brand Imagery is the intangible: brand personality, user imagery, usage situations, heritage, and values, meeting social and psychological needs.

## Level 3: Brand Response (judgments and feelings), What about you?

Response has two blocks. Brand Judgments are rational assessments: perceived quality, credibility, consideration, and superiority versus competitors. Brand Feelings are emotional reactions: warmth, fun, excitement, security, social approval, and self-respect.

## Level 4: Brand Resonance (relationships), What about you and me?

The apex is resonance, the deepest and hardest to reach: intense, active loyalty and psychological attachment. It shows up as behavioral loyalty (repeat buying), attitudinal attachment, sense of community, and active engagement. Resonance is where customers become advocates. Each level is cumulative and mutually reinforcing, building from awareness up to a genuine relationship.

title: Booms and Bitner, The 7Ps Extended Marketing Mix for Services
text:
## From 4Ps to 7Ps

In 1981, Booms and Bitner extended the traditional 4Ps marketing mix (Product, Price, Place, Promotion) by adding three elements for services: People, Process, and Physical Evidence. Together these form the extended, or services, marketing mix known as the 7Ps, which gained wide acceptance in services marketing.

## Why services need the extension

Services differ fundamentally from physical goods in four ways, which the original 4Ps did not adequately address:

Intangibility: services cannot be touched or seen before purchase, so buyers look for tangible cues.
Perishability: services cannot be stored or inventoried for later use, so capacity and demand must be managed in real time.
Inseparability: production and consumption happen simultaneously, so the customer is present during delivery.
Heterogeneity (variability): service quality varies by provider, time, and circumstances, so consistency is a challenge.

## The three added Ps

People: everyone directly or indirectly involved in delivering the service, including frontline staff and customer-facing employees, whose competence, behavior, and interpersonal skills shape the customer's perception of quality and satisfaction. It covers recruitment, culture, training, and remuneration.

Process: the procedures, mechanisms, and flow of activities by which the service is delivered, including sequence, time duration, and standardization. An effective, well-designed process is essential to service efficiency and a good customer experience.

Physical Evidence: the environment in which the service is delivered and all the tangibles that shape perceptions of the service and the firm, including facilities, equipment, signage, ambiance, and other environmental cues that let customers evaluate an intangible offering.

## Using the 7Ps

Because services are intangible and produced in front of the customer, People, Process, and Physical Evidence become controllable strategic variables just as important as the original four. The 7Ps is now often used as a generic marketing mix for both products and services.

title: Clayton Christensen, Jobs to Be Done and the Milkshake case
text:
## The central idea: customers hire products

Clayton Christensen's Jobs to Be Done theory holds that people essentially hire products to do a job for them. Rather than focusing on product features or customer demographics, the framework asks what progress the customer is trying to make. As Christensen put it, when people find themselves needing to get a job done, they essentially hire products to do that job for them. The question shifts from who the customer is to what job they are hiring the product for.

## The milkshake case study

A fast-food chain tried to grow milkshake sales through demographic research and product tweaks, making shakes more chocolatey, cheaper, chunkier, or chewier. Sales did not move. The breakthrough came from observing actual purchases: nearly half of milkshakes were sold before 8 a.m., the buyers were always alone, the milkshake was the only thing they bought, and they immediately drove away. The real job: relieving boredom on a long commute while staying full until mid-morning, with something that fits in a cupholder and can be consumed one-handed over 20 minutes. The true competition was not other milkshakes but bananas, donuts, bagels, and coffee.

## Three dimensions of a job

Every job has three dimensions: functional (the practical task to accomplish), emotional (how using the product makes the customer feel), and social (how it makes the customer look to others). Great products serve all three.

## Reframing segmentation

JTBD shifts segmentation away from who customers are (demographics) toward what progress they are trying to make. This reveals intent-driven motivation rather than demographic determinism, and it redefines the competitive set around the job, not the product category. It is a powerful antidote to marketing myopia, because it forces you to define the market by the customer's job, not by your product.

title: David Aaker, Managing Brand Equity: the Five Brand Assets
text:
## What brand equity is

David Aaker, in Managing Brand Equity (1991), defines brand equity as the set of assets and liabilities linked to a brand, its name and symbols, that add to or subtract from the value a product or service provides to customers and the firm. Aaker organizes these into five categories of brand assets.

## 1. Brand Loyalty

The strength of a customer's attachment to the brand. Loyalty reduces marketing and acquisition costs, boosts retention, provides time to respond to competitive moves, supports a price premium, and gives leverage with distribution. It is both an outcome of equity and a source of it.

## 2. Brand Awareness

The prominence of the brand in the buyer's mind: recognition and recall. Awareness aids consideration, signals substance and commitment, reduces search effort, and increases mental availability at the moment of decision. Aaker describes levels rising from recognition to top-of-mind.

## 3. Perceived Quality

The customer's perception of the overall quality or superiority of the brand relative to alternatives. Perceived quality influences willingness to buy, trial, price premium, and differentiation. It is often the single association most linked to financial performance.

## 4. Brand Associations

The linked thoughts, images, and feelings held in memory: attributes, benefits, values, personality, and experiences. Associations create meaning, differentiate the brand, provide reasons to buy, and are the basis of brand extensions.

## 5. Other Proprietary Brand Assets

Hard-to-replicate assets that reinforce competitive advantage: trademarks, patents, channel and distribution relationships, and other legally protected or exclusive elements. These prevent competitors from eroding the customer base and margins.

## Why the model matters

Aaker's five assets give marketers a structured way to diagnose brand strength, set priorities, and justify brand investment, treating the brand as a durable strategic asset rather than a cost.

title: Northwestern Medill (Don Schultz), What Is Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC)
text:
## What IMC is

Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) is a strategic framework that aligns brand marketing across all channels, uniting previously siloed departmental efforts under one data-driven, customer-centric umbrella. Instead of running advertising, PR, direct, digital, social, email, and sales promotion as separate silos, IMC coordinates them so the customer experiences one coherent brand.

## Don Schultz and the origin

The discipline was codified at Northwestern's Medill School by Professor Don Schultz, who in 1993 co-authored the first IMC textbook and moved the field from a tactical idea to a strategic management process. He recognized that treating each communication channel as a separate entity wasted resources and confused customers.

## The outside-in, customer-centric shift

IMC embodies a fundamental reorientation: the customer, not the brand, is the focus of all marketing efforts. This is a move from an inside-out, product-centered approach to an outside-in, audience-centered one that starts from customer data and behavior and works back to the message.

## Message consistency: one voice

The core principle is consistency. Every message and touchpoint can either build or erode brand equity, so all communications must carry a unified message and identity. Customers do not experience your advertising, PR, and email as separate departments; they experience one brand, and they notice immediately when it contradicts itself. Consistency compounds: it has been shown to increase brand popularity and fame measures.

## Channels coordinated

IMC integrates paid and earned media (advertising and PR), digital media and content, social, email, and SEO, and cross-platform campaigns, all with unified messaging and data-driven targeting so the brand speaks with one voice everywhere.

title: Jenni Romaniuk (Ehrenberg-Bass), Building Distinctive Brand Assets
text:
## What distinctive brand assets are

Distinctive brand assets, from Jenni Romaniuk and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, are the non-verbal cues that let buyers recognize a brand instantly without seeing its name: colors, shapes, packaging forms, type styles, characters and mascots, taglines, sonic cues, and motion. When category buyers reliably connect these sensory signals to your brand, you boost mental availability and increase the chance of being noticed and chosen. Assets work as retrieval cues in fast, context-triggered memory, so the brand surfaces first at the buying moment.

## The two key measures: Fame and Uniqueness

Fame is the percentage of category buyers who correctly attribute an asset to your brand when shown the asset without the brand name. High fame means the cue successfully retrieves your brand from memory.

Uniqueness is how exclusively the asset points to your brand rather than to competitors. Low uniqueness means the cue may also cue rivals, so spending on it can help competitors too.

## The Fame-Uniqueness grid

Assets plot into four quadrants. High fame and high uniqueness are core protective assets: deploy them prominently everywhere. High fame and low uniqueness are shared category cues: sharpen them or pair them with unique elements so you do not aid competitors. Low fame and high uniqueness are emerging assets: invest to build familiarity. Low fame and low uniqueness are non-assets: redesign or retire them to reduce clutter.

## Why distinctiveness beats differentiation

Ehrenberg-Bass argues that being distinctive (easy to recognize and mentally available) matters more for growth than being differentiated (meaningfully different on attributes), because most buying is low-attention and habitual. Distinctive assets ensure the brand is quickly identified and retrieved in cluttered categories and low-attention environments where buyers barely deliberate. Consistency over time is essential: changing your assets resets the memory work.

title: Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Category Entry Points and Mental Availability
text:
## What Category Entry Points are

Category Entry Points (CEPs) are the moments when someone mentally enters a product or service category: the cues, needs, and situations that trigger a buyer to think of brands. They are the thoughts and motives a buyer has when a buying occasion arises. For example, a sunny beach day can trigger thoughts of a refreshing drink, or hearing about savings on energy bills can trigger thoughts about solar panels. A single category has many CEPs, because people buy for many different reasons and occasions (to treat yourself, for the children, as a snack, to thank someone).

## CEPs are the building blocks of mental availability

Mental availability, the propensity of a brand to be thought of in buying situations, is built by linking the brand in memory to as many relevant CEPs as possible. The more often a brand pops up in the consumer's mind at relevant CEPs, the greater the chance of a future purchase. A brand's mental market share grows as it becomes associated with more of the situations that lead to buying.

## How CEPs drive growth

Growth comes from being brought to mind at more buying occasions, not just from being liked more by current buyers. Marketers should identify the important CEPs in their category, measure how strongly the brand is linked to each, and use advertising to build and refresh those memory links so the brand is retrieved first when the buyer next enters the category. This is the practical mechanism behind How Brands Grow: broaden the brand's network of buying-situation associations rather than narrowing to a single message.

## Practical use

A CEP audit maps the category's buying situations, often prompted by W-style questions (why buying, when, where, while doing what, with whom, and how feeling), then scores the brand's link strength to each. Weakly linked but high-frequency CEPs are the growth opportunities to target with communications.

title: Google Ads Help, About Attribution Models
text:
## What an attribution model is

An attribution model is the rule, or set of rules, that determines how much credit each ad interaction (or marketing touchpoint) gets for a conversion. It lets marketers see how ads work together across the customer journey rather than crediting only the final touch, which changes how you value channels and how you bid.

## The classic attribution models

Last Click: gives all credit for the conversion to the last-clicked ad and corresponding keyword. Simple, but it ignores every earlier interaction that helped.

First Click: gives all credit to the first ad interaction in the path. Useful for understanding demand generation, but overstates the opener.

Linear: distributes credit equally across all touchpoints in the conversion path.

Time Decay: gives more credit to interactions that happen closer in time to the conversion, using a half-life (commonly 7 days), so recent touches count more.

Position-Based (U-shaped): assigns 40 percent credit each to the first and last interactions, and spreads the remaining 20 percent across the middle interactions.

Data-Driven Attribution (DDA): distributes credit based on your account's actual past data for that conversion action, calculating the real contribution of each interaction across the path rather than using a fixed rule. Google has made DDA the default and deprecated the fixed first-click, linear, time-decay, and position-based models in its ads product, though last click remains available.

## Why it matters for a marketer

The choice of model changes which campaigns look effective, so it shapes budget allocation and bidding. Last-click flatters bottom-of-funnel activity and undercredits brand and upper-funnel work, which is one reason short-termism creeps in; multi-touch and data-driven models give a fairer read of how the whole funnel contributes.

title: Simon-Kucher, Value-Based Pricing
text:
## The three pricing logics

There are three basic ways to set a price. Cost-plus pricing starts from the cost of production and adds a markup, ignoring what the customer perceives. Competition-based pricing sets prices by reference to what competitors charge. Value-based pricing sets prices based on the perceived value of the product or service to the customer, so that prices align with the customer's willingness to pay.

## Value-based pricing defined

Simon-Kucher, a firm founded on pricing science, defines value-based pricing as setting prices according to the value customers perceive, not according to internal costs or historical prices. Willingness to pay, the maximum a customer will spend based on the benefits they perceive, is the central input. Understanding willingness to pay lets a company capture the benefits and unique value its product provides.

## Why value-based pricing wins

Value-based pricing typically produces higher profit margins than cost-plus or competitive methods, because it aligns price with customer-perceived benefit rather than merely covering cost plus markup. Cost-plus often leaves money on the table by failing to exploit willingness to pay, and can set prices too high or too low relative to what customers would actually pay.

## Anti-pattern: cost-plus by default and underpricing

Defaulting to cost-plus is a common mistake for differentiated, innovative, or brand-led products: it disconnects price from the value delivered and usually undercharges. Price is the single most powerful profit lever, so pricing to captured value (through research into willingness to pay, good-better-best tiering, and value communication) beats mechanically marking up cost. Cost-plus is only appropriate for true commodities, regulated markets, or undifferentiated offerings.

title: Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, How Do You Measure How Brands Grow (penetration and availability)
text:
## Penetration is the primary growth driver

The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute states plainly that brands mainly grow through penetration: expanding the number of buyers, rather than increasing loyalty among existing customers. So the first metric to watch is penetration (how many category buyers buy the brand at all in a period), not average frequency or loyalty rates, which tend to follow penetration by the Double Jeopardy Law.

## The two availabilities you must build and measure

Brand growth requires two interconnected elements. Mental availability is the ease with which buyers recall and recognize the brand in buying situations; it is built through easily recognizable, eye-catching distinctive brand assets and through associations with the reasons people buy. Physical availability is the brand being accessible in the variant, quantity, and price that match buyers' needs, through broad distribution and presence. A brand grows by improving both together.

## Category Entry Points as the association map

Beyond raw availability, the framework emphasizes connecting the brand to Category Entry Points, the various reasons and occasions consumers buy in a category (for chocolate: to treat yourself, for the children, as a snack, as a gift). Measuring the brand's link strength to each important CEP shows where mental availability can be grown.

## Measurement resources

Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow establishes the laws, and Jenni Romaniuk's Better Brand Health describes practical new metrics for assessing brand associations, mental availability, and distinctive-asset strength. The point is that brand health should be measured behaviorally (penetration, availability, CEP links), not just by attitudinal survey scores that mostly reflect current size.

title: Geoffrey Moore, Crossing the Chasm (technology adoption life cycle)
text:
## The Technology Adoption Life Cycle

Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm builds on Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovations. Adopters fall into five groups along a bell curve: Innovators (technology enthusiasts, about 2.5 percent), Early Adopters (visionaries, about 13.5 percent), Early Majority (pragmatists, about 34 percent), Late Majority (conservatives, about 34 percent), and Laggards (skeptics, about 16 percent). Each group has a distinct buying psychology.

## The chasm

The critical gap, the chasm, sits between the Early Adopters (visionaries) and the Early Majority (pragmatists). The two buy in fundamentally different ways. Early adopters are forgiving, willing to work through bugs, and buy for competitive advantage and to be first. The early majority is risk-averse: they wait for a proven, reliable, polished product and demand social proof, references, and industry-specific success stories before committing. A product that sells well to visionaries can stall and die in the chasm because pragmatist references do not yet exist.

## Crossing strategy: a beachhead niche and the whole product

Moore's prescription is to cross the chasm by targeting a single narrow niche market as a beachhead, rather than spreading thin across many segments. You dominate that one segment so completely that you own it and generate the word of mouth and references pragmatists in that niche trust, then expand into adjacent segments (the bowling-pin, or bowling-alley, strategy). Central to this is delivering the whole product: not just the core technology but the complete set of support, integrations, services, and case studies a pragmatist needs to adopt with confidence.

## Anti-pattern: treating pragmatists like visionaries

The classic failure is assuming momentum with early adopters will carry into the mainstream, and marketing to pragmatists with visionary messaging (raw innovation, being first). Pragmatists want proof and a complete, low-risk solution; selling them on novelty alone leaves the company stranded in the chasm.

title: EBSCO Research Starters, The AIDA Model (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action)
text:
## The AIDA model

AIDA is a hierarchy-of-effects model that describes the stages a consumer moves through toward a purchase: Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action. It is one of the oldest and most widely taught marketing and advertising frameworks, and it underlies the idea of the purchase funnel.

## The four stages

Attention (Awareness): capture the potential buyer's attention with striking visuals, a surprising fact, or an intriguing problem. You cannot influence someone who has not noticed you.

Interest: hold that attention with memorable, relevant content, storytelling, humor, or empathy, respecting limited attention spans and making the message relevant to the person.

Desire: move from liking to wanting by showing how the product meets the consumer's specific needs, using before-and-after demonstrations, proof, and use cases that build preference.

Action: prompt the purchase by clearly showing what to do next, where and how to buy, and often adding urgency, the step of closing the sale.

## Origin and the funnel

The model was developed by American marketer Elias St. Elmo Lewis around 1898, originally for direct selling, and refined by Edward Strong in the 1920s in The Psychology of Selling and Advertising. It is visualized as an inverted triangle or funnel, with the audience narrowing at each descending stage.

## Extensions and limits

Modern marketers extend AIDA with stages such as Retention (keeping interest and generating referrals) and Satisfaction (post-purchase contentment), reflecting that the journey does not end at the sale. AIDA's limitation is that it assumes a fairly linear, rational, single path to purchase; real journeys are non-linear and involve many touchpoints, which is why intent-based models (like See-Think-Do-Care) and evidence on out-of-market buyers complement it.

title: Bain and Company (Fred Reichheld), Net Promoter Score (NPS)
text:
## The Ultimate Question

Net Promoter Score (NPS), developed by Fred Reichheld and Bain and Company, is built on a single Ultimate Question: How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague? Respondents answer on a 0 to 10 scale. The idea is that willingness to recommend is a strong proxy for genuine loyalty and future growth, because people stake their own reputation when they refer.

## The three response groups

Promoters (score 9 to 10): loyal, enthusiastic fans who keep buying and refer others, fueling growth.
Passives (score 7 to 8): passively satisfied customers who are not enthusiastic and have lower repurchase and referral rates; they are vulnerable to competitors.
Detractors (score 0 to 6): unhappy customers who can damage the brand through negative word of mouth and who churn at higher rates.

## The calculation

NPS equals the percentage of Promoters minus the percentage of Detractors. Passives are counted in the total but do not add to the score. The result is a number that can range from minus 100 (all detractors) to plus 100 (all promoters).

## What NPS is used for

NPS gives a clear, comparable measure of performance through customers' eyes. Organizations track it across business units, products, locations, teams, customer segments, and regions to spot where to improve, and manage toward creating more promoters and fewer detractors. In the full Net Promoter System, the score is paired with closed-loop follow-up (finding out why customers gave their score and acting on it), not treated as a vanity number on its own.

## Caveat for marketers

NPS is a useful relationship and loyalty signal, but it is a survey attitude measure and should be read alongside behavioral evidence (penetration, repeat rate, retention). Chasing the score itself, rather than the underlying customer experience, turns it into a vanity metric.

title: Think with Google, Decoding Decisions: the Messy Middle of the purchase journey
text:
## The messy middle

Google's Decoding Decisions research describes real buying behavior as happening in the messy middle: the complex space between a trigger and a purchase, where customers are won and lost. It is not a linear funnel. In a world of abundant choice and limitless information, people loop through the middle repeatedly before they buy.

## Two mental modes: exploration and evaluation

Within the messy middle, consumers move between two mental modes. Exploration is an expansive activity: gathering information and adding brands and products to a consideration set, across search, social, aggregators, and review sites. Evaluation is a reductive activity: weighing and narrowing the options. People cycle between exploration and evaluation, expanding and contracting their consideration set, until they are ready to act.

## Six cognitive biases

To cope with complexity, people lean on cognitive biases. Google prioritized six that most influence buying: category heuristics (short descriptions of key specifications simplify the choice), power of now (the longer you must wait for something, the weaker the proposition), social proof (recommendations and reviews from others are persuasive), scarcity bias (as availability drops, desirability rises), authority bias (being swayed by an expert or trusted source), and power of free (a free gift with purchase is a strong motivator).

## What marketers should do

The practical implications: build and maintain brand presence so you are already in the consideration set when exploration begins (this connects to mental availability), be present and easy to evaluate at the evaluation stage, close the gap between trigger and purchase efficiently, and apply behavioral-science principles responsibly rather than manipulatively. The messy middle reframes the job from pushing people down a funnel to being consistently present and easy to choose throughout a looping, non-linear journey.

title: Core Marketing Metrics: CAC, LTV, ROAS, ROMI, MQL, SQL, Conversion Rate
text:
## Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)

CAC is the total expense to acquire one new customer, including all marketing and sales costs. Formula: CAC equals total marketing plus sales spend, divided by the number of new customers acquired in the period. Lower CAC means more efficient acquisition, but it must always be read against the value a customer brings.

## Customer Lifetime Value (LTV or CLV)

LTV is the total revenue a customer generates across the entire relationship with the business. A higher LTV justifies more aggressive acquisition spending. A common expansion of the formula is average order value times purchase frequency times gross margin times average customer lifespan.

## LTV to CAC ratio

This compares lifetime value to acquisition cost and is the headline efficiency benchmark. A healthy ratio is around 3 to 1 or higher, meaning LTV should be at least three times CAC. Much higher than 5 to 1 can signal underinvestment in growth; below 3 to 1 signals acquisition is too expensive relative to value.

## Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) and Return on Marketing Investment (ROMI)

ROAS is revenue generated for every unit of paid ad spend. Formula: revenue generated divided by ad spend. A 4 to 1 ROAS means every ad dollar generates 4 dollars of revenue. ROMI is broader: (marketing-attributed revenue minus marketing costs) divided by marketing costs, times 100, expressed as a percentage.

## MQL and SQL

A Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL) is a lead that meets criteria (demographics, behavior, engagement) indicating higher purchase intent and readiness to be passed to sales. A Sales Qualified Lead (SQL) is a lead that sales has vetted and confirmed as ready for direct sales engagement. The MQL-to-SQL handoff measures lead quality and marketing-to-sales alignment.

## Conversion rate

Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors (or leads) who complete a desired action. Formula: conversions divided by total visitors, times 100. It is tracked at every funnel stage to find where prospects drop off.

## Anti-pattern: vanity metrics

A top marketer distinguishes vanity metrics (impressions, raw followers, page views, likes) from actionable metrics tied to revenue and efficiency (CAC, LTV to CAC, ROAS, ROMI, pipeline, conversion rate). Big numbers that do not connect to business outcomes flatter reports without informing decisions. Every metric should support a decision and, ideally, ladder up to profit and durable growth, not just short-term response.
